solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Compose, from lace, beautiful bags, after retiring

indicators.note: retiring means going backwards, so the held letters are read in reverse
the run of words 'from lace, beautiful' bags, or holds, a run of letters inside it

explanation.surface: A dressmaker composes something beautiful out of lace, then retires for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bags' marks letters held within 'froM LACE, Beautiful', giving MLACEB; 'after retiring' turns those letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: To compose oneself or another is to quieten and settle, the verb sense of making still.

clue.text: Subtle manoeuvres with club coach during campaign

parts.note: a bat is a club used in sport

indicators.note: manoeuvres means the letters are moved about into new positions

explanation.surface: A subtle coach manoeuvres with a club during a season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coach' looks like a sports trainer; it is a bus used to tour a candidate around in an election.
explanation.definitionFit: A party's touring vehicle in an election campaign is the bus that carries its leader.

clue.text: Mustard for one's heart, so they say

indicators.note: so they say means the word is taken by how it is spoken

parts.note: a kernel is the heart or core of something

explanation.surface: Mustard is said to be good for your heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Mustard is a character in the board game Cluedo (Clue in the US).
explanation.definitionFit: Mustard is the rank-holding army officer among the Cluedo suspects, so an example of the title.

clue.text: Put down endless bags — one's not cloth)

parts.note: to lay is to put down

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

parts.note: bags of something means lots, many

explanation.surface: Someone lays down bags without end; he's no member of the cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the cloth' means the clergy, so a person not of the cloth is not ordained.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the congregation who is not ordained clergy is a non-clerical person.

clue.text: Start to smile? Not true

parts.note: 'they're off' marks the start of a race, so off can mean starting
a beam is a broad smile

explanation.surface: Is beginning to smile a sign that something isn't true?
explanation.definitionFit: Something wide of the mark or mistaken is inaccurate, the informal sense of off line.

clue.text: Cat spotted crumb?

definitions.meaning: the snow leopard, a spotted big cat of Central Asia, has this name
a crumb is a tiny amount

explanation.surface: Did the cat spot a crumb?
explanation.definitionFit: The snow leopard bears this name, and the weight also means the smallest scrap of something.

clue.text: Line crossed by go-getter, the source of quarrel?

indicators.note: the line is crossed, i.e. held across the middle, by the other word

parts.note: a fetcher is one who goes and gets things

explanation.surface: A line is crossed by an ambitious person, causing a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarrel' looks like an argument; it is a crossbow bolt.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrow maker produces arrows and crossbow bolts, so is where a quarrel comes from.

clue.text: Terminal on fixture, a shade old, to corrode

indicators.note: terminal on asks for the end letter of the word that follows

parts.note: a tint is a shade of colour

explanation.surface: Fitting an old-shaded terminal on a fixture to stop corrosion.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid will gradually wear away or erode metal, the phrasal-verb sense of corrode.

clue.text: Gravy's goodness: I should tuck in!

indicators.note: tucking in means fitting inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: my! is an exclamation like goodness!
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: The gravy's so good, I should tuck in!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gravy' looks like the sauce; it is slang for easy cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Gravy is informal for easy profit or cash, a slang synonym for wealth.

clue.text: Capable of meeting boyfriend now?

definitions.meaning: 'up to' means capable of, and a date is a meeting with a boyfriend

explanation.surface: Is she ready to meet the boyfriend now?
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means modern or current, and read in parts says equal to a romantic outing.

clue.text: Form of media report unknown

parts.note: to tell is to report or relate
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknown quantities

explanation.surface: A form of media reports something unknown.
explanation.walkthrough: TELLY is British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: Television is a broadcast medium, and this is its everyday British nickname.

clue.text: Private Eye, like the FT, not about to backtrack

parts.note: the Financial Times is printed on pink paper

indicators.note: backtracking means going back the way you came, so these letters run in reverse

parts.note: taken as written
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A dig at Private Eye, the satirical magazine, compared with the Financial Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private Eye' looks like the magazine; it means a private detective. Allan Pinkerton founded a famous US detective agency.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pinkerton agent was a private detective, which a private eye is in slang.

clue.text: Tenor needs something mechanical to reach holiday island

parts.note: Mario Lanza was a famous American tenor
rote is mechanical repetition, learning by heart without thought

explanation.surface: A singer needs some machine to get him to a holiday island.
explanation.definitionFit: This Canary Island is a popular European sun resort, a holiday destination.

clue.text: Fly from US city after reduction in staff

indicators.note: the city's letters come after the shortened staff
the word is reduced, cut short by its final letter

parts.note: a cane is a walking stick or staff
NY is New York

explanation.surface: Someone flies out of an American city after being made redundant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a verb about air travel; here it is the adjective meaning shrewd.
explanation.definitionFit: Fly in informal British use means knowing and sharp, the same as shrewd.

clue.text: Warning sound maybe dish picked up

indicators.note: picked up means heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a dish is slang for an attractive person, a belle

explanation.surface: A dish being picked up might give a warning sound.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm or alert can be rung out by this, so it is an example of a warning signal.

clue.text: Used to drink after writing note

indicators.note: the drinking word follows the other two

parts.note: a hand is a style of handwriting
me (or mi) is the third note of the sol-fa scale
to down a drink is to swallow it

explanation.surface: Someone used to have a drink after writing a note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to' reads as a habit; 'Used' alone is the definition, meaning second-hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes passed on from an older sibling are second-hand, previously worn.

clue.text: Fellow hugging one girl is lifting arm

indicators.note: hugging means holding inside, so the fellow wraps the other letters

parts.note: a don is a university fellow
I is the Roman numeral one
Vi is short for the girl's name Violet

indicators.note: in a down answer, lifting means the word is read upwards, in reverse

explanation.surface: A fellow hugging a girl is raising his arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arm' looks like a limb; it is a branch of the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: An army unit, or a branch of an organisation, is a section of it, like an arm.

clue.text: Around the corner, child seen outside betting club

parts.note: nigh means near, just around the corner

indicators.note: the child is seen outside, wrapping the betting letters

parts.note: a tot is a small child
SP is the starting price in horse-race betting

explanation.surface: Around the corner, a child is seen outside a betting shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' looks like a sports or gambling club; it is a nightclub.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightclub is a venue open late for entertainment, also called a club.

clue.text: Mark — or email, exceptionally — serving as reminder

parts.note: M stands for mark, the old German currency

indicators.note: exceptionally means out of the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An email, unusually, serves to remind someone named Mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A commemorative object or occasion recalls something to mind, so it is a reminder.

clue.text: During which sailors rest, or else have reels

indicators.note: to reel is to stagger and spin, so the letters whirl into a new order

explanation.surface: Sailors on rest days either relax or dance reels.
explanation.definitionFit: Time off granted to a ship's crew to go on land is this, so it is when they rest.

clue.text: A bad thing to do to welcome wrong guy

definitions.text: A bad thing to do to welcome

parts.note: out means wrong, as in 'your guess is out'
a guy is a rope holding something steady, also called a stay

explanation.surface: Welcoming the wrong guy is a bad thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: You would 'outstay your welcome', a bad thing to do to a welcome.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying longer than wanted spoils a host's welcome, the idiom 'outstay your welcome'.

clue.text: Deal in fact leaving out government at first

indicators.note: at first asks for the opening letter of each of the four words before it

explanation.surface: Trading on the fact that the government has been left out at first.
explanation.walkthrough: FLOG is British slang for sell.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog goods is informal British for selling them, so to trade or deal in them.

clue.text: Plain person quite bowled over by legendary fiddler

indicators.note: by means next to, so the fiddler comes beside the first piece
bowled over means knocked upside down, so in a down answer the word reads upwards

parts.note: quite and all both mean completely
Nero is said to have fiddled while Rome burned

explanation.surface: Someone plain is quite overwhelmed by a legendary violinist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like ordinary; it means grassland: the llanos of South America.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy or inhabitant of the South American grassland plains is a plainsman.

clue.text: US actor and singer to combine with orchestra for one

indicators.note: for means in place of, so the orchestra replaces the one

parts.note: join means combine
I is the Roman numeral one
LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra

explanation.surface: An American star joins forces with an orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: Al Jolson starred in The Jazz Singer, the first feature-length talkie.
explanation.definitionFit: Al Jolson was a famous American entertainer of stage and screen.

clue.text: The same song, but with different ending

indicators.note: the song's last letter is swapped for another letter

parts.note: a ditty is a short simple song

explanation.surface: It's the same song again, only the ending has changed.
explanation.walkthrough: The new letter is not clued; crossing letters supply it.
explanation.definitionFit: This word is used to say that something repeats what was said before, the same thing again.

clue.text: Find Barb cheerful

parts.note: a dig is a barbed remark
up means in good spirits

explanation.surface: A man called Barb seems cheerful.
explanation.definitionFit: To unearth or discover information is to uncover it, the phrasal sense of find.

clue.text: Firm's way of working: head to bring in a long-distance traveller

parts.note: co is short for company, a firm, plus 's
MO is modus operandi, a way of working

indicators.note: the head word brings in, or contains, the letter A

parts.note: nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A company's working practice: the boss brings in someone who travels far.
explanation.definitionFit: A Soviet or Russian space traveller journeys vast distances into orbit.

clue.text: Steal fawn

definitions.meaning: to steal is to move quietly and secretly
to fawn is to grovel or toady

explanation.surface: Steal a young deer.
explanation.definitionFit: To move stealthily and to suck up obsequiously are both senses of this verb.

clue.text: To twig, see in a new light?

definitions.text: To twig, see in a new light?

indicators.note: seeing words in a new light means rearranging them, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: To understand something, you look at it from a fresh angle.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to become aware of or catch on, the informal sense of twig.

clue.text: One easily led escape, slowly straddling horse

indicators.note: straddling means sitting astride, so one word goes round the letter

parts.note: to seep is to leak out slowly
H is slang for heroin, which is also called horse

explanation.surface: A rider slowly escapes, astride a horse that is easily led.
explanation.definitionFit: A docile follower who goes along with the flock is called this, as an idiom.

clue.text: Isn't genuinely appreciating when this note accompanies service

definitions.text: Isn't genuinely appreciating when this note accompanies service

parts.words: Isn't genuinely appreciating when this note accompanies service
parts.note: a wage slip is a note; put before the word service it makes the idiom for insincere praise

explanation.surface: Insincere appreciation of good service in a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer in two and add 'service' to get the idiom for praise without meaning it.
explanation.definitionFit: A salary statement is a note handed to an employee, and the cryptic reading builds the idiom.

clue.text: No wheels: settle for walking or running

indicators.note: to wheel is to turn round, so the word is turned back to front

parts.note: taken as written
to foot a bill is to settle it

explanation.surface: No car: you'll have to make do with walking or running.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling by leg rather than vehicle, the idiom for going by pedestrian means.
